endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Moreover, when the end user of an AI solution lacks the necessary education or background to understand the output, accuracy, risks, and limitations of the AI output, the situation presents another risk to be considered, measured, and managed appropriately.

commentary.bottom_line: One industry framework, the CHAI Responsible AI Guide, recommends that deployment risk assessments account for end users who lack the background to understand AI output accuracy, risks, and limitations. No study supplied here tests this practice or documents the hazard it targets, so the recommendation rests on expert consensus alone.

perspectives.view: No study tests whether adding user-understanding risk to deployment assessments changes how outputs are interpreted or used, and no study documents the size of the hazard. Under GRADE conventions the certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The recommendation reflects a single framework's judgment rather than tested effect.

The sole endorsement comes from the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide, a voluntary industry framework that uses "should" language. The supplied material contains no statute, FDA guidance, or ONC rule that requires this item in a risk assessment. Health systems that adopt it would do so as a voluntary practice.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without a documented assessment of user background and literacy, measuring misinterpretation of AI outputs, override errors, and downstream patient harm. Baseline studies that measure how often clinicians and patients misread AI accuracy and limitation statements would also establish whether the hazard is common enough to warrant routine assessment.
commentary.underserved_note: No study was supplied, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The recommendation's concern with users who lack background knowledge may apply with particular force to these groups, but the evidence base offers no information on how the practice performs for them.
